title: What not to put on the site for an education product
metaTitle: Education product website mistakes to cut
excerpt: Cut the badge dashboard, the fear, and the extra pages. Keep the learning moment and a way to start. A shorter site that tells the truth wins.

faqs.question: What should an education site cut first?
faqs.answer: The badge dashboard on the first screen, then fear-based headlines, then unnamed quotes and undefined learning gains. Keep the learning moment and a way to start a class or a trial. The dashboard comforts the team and confuses the buyer.

faqs.question: How short can the site be?
faqs.answer: Home, a door for teachers, a door for families, pricing, one proof page, a true about page, and a start path can be complete. Add writing only when a real buyer asked a question those pages could not answer. Shorter still has to tell the truth about price and lesson.

faqs.question: What should replace a logo wall?
faqs.answer: One story with a constraint and a screen, or the screen alone until you have permission. A wall of school logos that does not open onto a lesson teaches the buyer to expect the same emptiness in the product.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Cut the dashboard full of badges. It is the most common of the education product website mistakes: it reassures the team and confuses a teacher or a parent with little time. Keep the learning moment and a clear way to start a class or a trial. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long one that performs taste.

Those are the mistakes that matter. The other clutter is usually there so the team can avoid showing the lesson.

## The badge dashboard

Streaks, points, leaderboards, and trophies on the first screen answer a company question: do people come back. The parent asked a different question: will my child practice reading. The teacher asked whether this fits a period and shows who is stuck. A wall of badges makes the product look like a game about itself. The lesson is somewhere underneath, easy to miss, easy to close.

Replace it with one scene. The sentence a child tries. The hint after a miss. The short list a teacher checks. If encouragement belongs in the product, show the quiet line after a hard step, not a trophy case. The picture will be remembered. Make it the lesson.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is why this cut comes first. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. A page has to show its value in about 10 seconds to earn a longer look, and readers get through only about a quarter of the text. A badge wall plus a mission plus a logo row spends that budget before the lesson appears. Write the quarter. Delete the rest of the hero.

If the team is attached to the dashboard, caption each widget with the decision it helps a teacher or a parent make. The widgets that cannot take a caption are the ones to remove from the marketing page. You will usually find that one list, or one exercise, was doing the real work. Lead with that. Let the analytics live inside the product for the people who already have a class.

## A long site that performs taste

Extra pages feel serious in a deck. On the site they become places to hide vague writing. A manifesto about the future of learning. A culture page. A post for every synonym of your skill. A "community" that is a newsletter archive. None of these help a parent start tonight or a teacher start Monday. They help a team sound larger than the lesson.

[A study of generative search visibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) measured about a ten percent drop when pages stuffed repeated phrases, and it found gains for citations, quotations, and statistics you can actually support. You do not need to write for a machine to use the lesson. Repeating "learning" in every heading makes the page harder for a person to quote, too. One moment, said once, with the grade and the skill named, is enough.

Keep the pages that match jobs. Home. For teachers. For families. Pricing. One or two proof pages. About, if it names who edits the lessons. A contact or start path. Add writing only when a real buyer asked a question those pages could not answer. Do not add it because a calendar said to publish.

Shorter does not mean coy. The remaining pages have to do their jobs. The homepage shows the moment and the start. Pricing shows what is included and what is not. The start path says what happens next. A short page that still hides the price or the lesson is not the shorter site this piece means. It is a teaser. Teasers waste the little time this buyer has.

## Jargon and fear before the lesson

Cut the abstract nouns. Pathways. Ecosystems. Outcomes. Engagement. Personalized at scale. These words are how a product avoids saying "fractions" or "a ten-minute reading practice." The specific skill feels smaller inside the company and clearer outside it. Clarity is the sale. The abstraction is the mistake.

Cut fear. "Don't let them fall behind." "While you wait, the gap grows." Parents have enough fear. A homepage that opens on it is using the child as pressure. Show the work the child will do. Adults can decide if it matters. You will lose some impulse signups and keep more trust. Take that trade.

Cut claims you cannot point at. A learning-gain percentage with no defined group. "Built by educators" when the editors are not named. "Trusted by thousands of schools" when the logos are pilots, friends, or hopes. A quote you rewrote. If a number is true and you may share it, put it on the proof page with the definition in the same breath. If it is not, delete it. Teachers repeat numbers. They also repeat the discovery that a number was theater.

Cut fake urgency. Spots left in a cohort that is not a cohort. Countdown timers on a trial. "Enrolling now" banners that have been up all year. A true sentence, that school conversations are booking for a later month, is allowed because it is capacity. A timer is a costume, and this buyer has seen it on worse products.

## Proof and navigation that do not help

Cut the testimonial slider of unnamed stars. Cut the school logo wall that does not open onto a learning moment. Cut a case study that is a metric and a handshake. Publish one story with a constraint, a decision, and the screen, or publish the screen alone until you have permission to tell the story. Weak proof is worse than a gap, because it teaches the buyer what to expect from the product.

Cut department names in the bar. Platform. Resources. Community. Solutions. Use jobs: for teachers, for families, pricing, start a class, start a trial. Cut duplicate starts. A demo button, a sales button, a free button, and a chat, all in the same view. Pick the door. Put the others behind the label that matches the buyer, not in a row of competing verbs.

Cut the blog from the main path if it does not help someone decide to start. Articles can be good and still be a detour. A detour that ranks for a neighboring phrase and then offers no lesson is still a mistake. Link a truly useful piece from the page it supports. Leave the rest out of the bar.

Cut password walls and "request a demo to see the product." The learning moment is the product. If a parent has to book a call to see a reading exercise, you have built a moat in front of the only evidence you had. Show the exercise. Save the call for the school path that actually needs one.

## What teams keep because it feels safe

Teams keep the badges because a plain exercise looks small. Small is the point. A ten-minute practice that a parent understands is easier to start than a platform that needs a tour. The fear of looking small is an internal fear. Do not make the buyer pay for it with confusion.

They keep pages because someone spent a week on the manifesto. The week is gone either way. Removing the nav item stops every future visitor from paying for it too. Archive the draft. The site is not a memorial for effort.

They keep stock children pointing at blank screens because a real crop of the product feels unfinished. If the product frame is unfinished, finish the product frame. A stock child will not survive the trial, where the real screen appears. Match the ad to the build. Hanabi designs and builds so the marketing picture and the interface can be the same decision. If your teams are separate, give them one sentence they both have to obey: the lesson before the badge.

They keep motion that delays the words. An entrance for the headline. A video of a classroom with the sound off and no captions. Let the sentence be present immediately. Then show the product. Reduced motion should show the same lesson, not a broken leftover. Care with motion is part of whether you seem safe to put in front of a child.

## A shorter site

A practical cut for a weekend:

- Remove the badge dashboard from the first screen. Put one captioned learning moment there.
- Remove fear, fake numbers, and unnamed quotes.
- Remove nav items that are not jobs.
- Remove form fields until only role, grade or skill, and email remain for a trial.
- Remove pages that repeat another page in vaguer words.
- Read what is left on a phone. If the lesson and the start are visible quickly, stop.

Then read it as a parent, and again as a teacher. You should be able to say what the learner does, what it does not do, and how to begin. If you can say those three things, another page will not raise the chance of a fair trial. It will raise the chance of a mixed message.

What remains is enough. A first screen with the lesson. A door for families and a door for teachers. A price shape. Proof with a constraint. People who edit the work. Pictures of the step, not of a trophy. A start path that lands in the product. A phone layout that was designed on a phone.

Hanabi's stack, Next.js and TypeScript and a fast public site, is only relevant here as a standard: the page should load the lesson before it loads a performance. You do not need to name the tools to your buyers. You need to refuse the heavy hero. Ordinary and true beats a long site that performs taste.

## What to write next, after the cuts

After the cuts, look at the path a stranger actually walks. They arrive, they judge, they start, or they leave. The pages that do not sit on that walk can wait. The pages that do should be specific enough that another person could quote the decision.

The same standard shows up when the site's job is to bring the right projects in, rather than the right class. [How a studio website gets inbound leads](/blog/how-a-studio-website-gets-inbound-leads) is the next piece if you are also shaping the studio's own front door. Read it for the habit, not for a second dose of urgency. One clear offer, proof that shows a decision, and a way to begin. Then stop adding blocks that only comfort the team.

If you want help choosing what to remove, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice how little a strong page needs once the decision is visible. Bring your current homepage to that standard. Cut the dashboard. Keep the lesson. Let a teacher or a parent start.
